steps.intent: The United States aims to secure a strong humanitarian and civilian-protection resolution that condemns RSF atrocities, demands a nationwide ceasefire and unhindered access, supports accountability, and reaffirms the sanctions regime without imposing new mandatory measures that would invite a Russian veto. The main difficulties will be Russian and Chinese objections to naming the RSF too directly or adding Chapter VII-style enforcement, Sudanese sensitivity over sovereignty and cross-border access, and debates over accountability language and any new sanctions or reporting requirements. We have therefore kept the draft balanced enough to attract at least nine votes while preserving core U.S. priorities.

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports the draft's ceasefire and humanitarian objectives and can support it with amendments. We ask the penholder to acknowledge the Government of Sudan's positive decisions on Adré and humanitarian air operations, to avoid language that places the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF on an equal footing, and to anchor humanitarian access in respect for Sudan's sovereignty. We also seek safeguards in OP8 on any additional measures, including humanitarian exemptions and consultation with Sudan and regional partners.
messages.China: China supports the draft's core objectives on ceasefire, protection of civilians and humanitarian access. We ask the penholder to revise OP4 to respect Sudan's sovereignty and national laws, and OP8 to ensure any further measures are considered only in full consultation with the Government of Sudan and regional organizations. We also need a clear reference to Sudanese ownership and thorough consultations with the Government of Sudan, consistent with the Council's previous discussions.
messages.Denmark: Denmark thanks the United States for a strong and balanced draft and supports its core demands. We ask that OP3 condemn indiscriminate SAF airstrikes as clearly as RSF attacks, that OP6 add cooperation with the International Criminal Court to the accountability language, and that OP7 include respect for South Sudan's sovereignty and territorial integrity given the regional spillover. These changes would strengthen the Council's consistency on protection of civilians and accountability; we can otherwise support the text.
messages.France: France supports this draft as a good basis and thanks the United States for circulating it. We ask that the ceasefire demand be placed explicitly under Chapter VII and that OP1 refer to the Secretary-General's Personal Envoy, Mr. Lamamra. We also seek firmer language in OP6 on accountability, including cooperation with the ICC on Darfur, and in OP7 on external support and strict compliance with the arms embargo. France remains ready to work constructively so that the Council can speak with one voice and avoid another veto.
messages.Greece: Greece supports the draft's core humanitarian, protection and accountability messages. We ask the penholder to add an explicit reference to starvation as a method of warfare in OP2 and to include the International Criminal Court among accountability mechanisms in OP6, consistent with the Darfur referral and EU positions. We can support the text with these adjustments.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the draft's balanced focus on ceasefire, humanitarian access, protection of civilians and accountability. We ask that OP8 make clear that any additional measures are targeted and subject to fair and clear procedures, and that OP3 use equally obligatory language for the SAF's obligations under international humanitarian law. We remain committed to working with the penholder to maintain Council unity on Sudan.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the draft’s core objectives: an immediate ceasefire, protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access and a Sudanese-owned political process. We request that OP8 make clear that any additional measures must be targeted, criteria-based and due-process compliant and must not hamper humanitarian assistance, and that OP9 include the OIC given its role in support of Sudan. With these adjustments, Pakistan can support the text.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the thrust of the draft and its balanced focus on protection of civilians, humanitarian access and accountability. We ask the penholder to make the humanitarian commitments more operational by adding immediate humanitarian pauses and concrete cross-border and deconfliction language. We also suggest that the Secretary-General's reporting explicitly cover access impediments, so the Council can follow up.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the draft's core objectives and its balanced call on the parties. As Chair of the 1591 Committee, we would like the text to translate concern over arms embargo violations into stronger implementation language and to add a concrete follow-up role for the Committee and Panel. We also ask the penholder to make the humanitarian access provisions more operational by citing the Adré crossing and lifting time restrictions.
messages.Russian Federation: We thank the United States for its work, but the current text remains unbalanced and contains elements that prejudge Sudan's sovereignty and national processes. Our red lines are equal condemnation of attacks by all parties, no endorsement of the HRC fact-finding mission without Sudanese consent, and no language that could be used against legitimate bilateral cooperation with the Government of Sudan. We are ready to work constructively, but these changes are necessary for us to support the draft.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the draft as a strong basis and welcomes its focus on cessation of hostilities, humanitarian access, and accountability. We would like the text to carry forward the Council's call in resolution 2736 for the Secretary-General to consult on recommendations for protecting civilians, and to ensure balanced demands on all parties, including the SAF, while explicitly addressing conflict-related sexual violence and grave violations against children. These changes reflect our national experience and our consistent priority on protection of civilians in Sudan.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the draft as a good basis and thanks the United States for its pen. We ask for stronger and more balanced international humanitarian law language in OP3, explicit access to El Fasher and Zamzam and the lifting of sieges in OP4, and an ICC cooperation call in OP6. These changes are important for the protection of civilians and accountability, and we are flexible on precise formulation.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the draft as presented. We welcome its balanced emphasis on Sudan's sovereignty and territorial integrity, humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and an inclusive Sudanese-led political process with a central role for the African Union and IGAD. We encourage the penholder to keep close coordination with regional partners during implementation and reporting.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom thanks the United States for its leadership and broadly supports this text. We would like targeted amendments to make clear that civilians must be allowed to leave besieged areas safely, that the Adré crossing must be urgently reopened and sustained, and that external support enhancing either side’s fighting capability must be condemned. We also seek a modest strengthening of accountability language for war crimes and other serious violations.

replies.Greece: partially accepted: starvation language added in OP2; ICC reference not included.
replies.Guyana: partially accepted: OP8 now targeted and subject to fair and clear procedures; SAF language remains calls upon rather than demands.
replies.Pakistan: accepted: OP8 safeguards and OIC reference included.
replies.Panama: accepted: humanitarian pauses, cross-border routes from Chad and South Sudan, deconfliction, and reporting on access obstacles included.
replies.Republic of Korea: partially accepted: Adré, time restrictions, and 1591 Committee engagement included; explicit additional designations language omitted.
replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: balanced condemnation, removal of Fact-Finding welcome, sovereignty language, and deletion of explicit new-measures readiness; concern on arms transfers retained and no consent requirement added.
replies.Sierra Leone: partially accepted: SG recommendations on protection of civilians and stronger sexual violence language included; OP8 designation expansion not included.
replies.Slovenia: partially accepted: strengthened siege, El Fasher/Zamzam, and starvation language; ICC cooperation not included.
replies.Somalia: accepted: no changes requested; core sovereignty, humanitarian and regional coordination language retained.
replies.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: partially accepted: civilian evacuation from besieged areas, Adré, and war crimes accountability included; external support language expresses concern rather than condemnation.

steps.summary: The revision balances US priorities on humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and accountability with key Russian and Chinese concerns, including balanced condemnation, sovereignty language, and removal of explicit new-measures language. It retains existing sanctions and 1591 Committee engagement, and is expected to secure broad support with Russia abstaining.

messages.Algeria: Algeria welcomes the incorporation of the Adré language, the sovereignty and coordination language in OP4, and the OP8 safeguards, and supports the draft as a basis. We remain concerned that OP3 should not place the Government of Sudan and the RSF on an equal footing; it should reaffirm the Government’s primary responsibility to protect civilians while demanding compliance by all parties. We also ask that OP8 expressly provide for engagement with the Government of Sudan and regional partners to avoid unintended humanitarian consequences. With these adjustments, Algeria can vote in favour.
messages.China: China supports the revised draft as a basis and welcomes the incorporation of sovereignty, consultation and Sudanese ownership language. To enable our support, OP4 should avoid language that reads as imposing obligations on the Government of Sudan and should be recast around facilitation consistent with Sudan’s sovereignty and national laws. We appreciate the penholder’s continued flexibility and hope this remaining concern can be addressed.
messages.Denmark: Denmark thanks the penholder for strengthening the balanced IHL language and for including South Sudan and neighbouring States in OP7. We continue to seek an explicit accountability hook in OP6 to the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan and the International Criminal Court, reflecting the Darfur referral and the need to end impunity. With that addition, Denmark is ready to support the draft.
messages.France: France thanks the United States for the revised text and welcomes the inclusion of the Personal Envoy and the strengthened language on external interference. For France, the Council’s demands must be binding and accountability for Darfur must be explicit; we therefore ask for a Chapter VII reference before OP1 and an ICC cooperation clause in OP6. We also seek an upgrade in OP7 from 'calls upon' to 'demands' regarding external interference, including financial and logistical support. With these adjustments, France can support the resolution.
messages.Greece: Greece welcomes the inclusion of language on starvation of civilians in OP2. We continue to believe that OP6 should explicitly reference the International Criminal Court, consistent with the Council’s prior referral on Darfur and the need to end impunity. Greece can support the text with this amendment.
messages.Guyana: Guyana welcomes the revision to OP8 and the draft’s reaffirmation of Sudan’s sovereignty and of African-led coordination. We continue to believe OP3 should apply the same binding language to the SAF as to the RSF, because equal treatment of the parties is essential to the resolution’s credibility and implementation. Guyana is prepared to support the text with that adjustment and urges the penholder to reflect it in the final revision.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the revised draft. We welcome the inclusion of due-process and humanitarian safeguards in OP8 and the OIC reference in OP9. We encourage the Council to maintain a unified message in support of Sudan’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and a Sudanese-led political process, and we will vote in favour.
messages.Panama: Panama welcomes revision 1 and thanks the penholder for incorporating our priorities on immediate humanitarian pauses, cross-border access from Chad and South Sudan, humanitarian deconfliction, and reporting on access obstacles. The text is balanced, grounded in international humanitarian law and Sudanese sovereignty, and provides a workable basis for Council action. Panama therefore supports the draft and calls on all parties to comply fully with its demands.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the current text and appreciates the penholder's incorporation of our key requests, including the Adré crossing, lifting time restrictions on cross-border access, and strengthened engagement by the 1591 Committee. While we would have preferred explicit language on considering additional designations, we recognize the balanced compromise reflected in OP8 on applying existing listing criteria and fair procedures. Given the urgency of Council action on Sudan, we will support the draft as it stands.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation cannot support the current text, which still contains unbalanced demands and accusatory language on arms transfers and external support. We insist on deleting the one-sided RSF/SAF-specific clause in OP3 and the unfounded concern in OP7, and on ensuring that humanitarian and accountability language fully respects Sudan's sovereignty and the consent of its Government. Without these red-line corrections, we will not be in a position to support the draft.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone welcomes the inclusion of our proposed language on the Secretary-General's recommendations on protection of civilians and on survivor-centered accountability. We continue to believe that the Council must be even-handed: OP3 should demand, not merely call upon, that the SAF comply with international humanitarian law and refrain from indiscriminate airstrikes. We also ask that OP8 reflect the Committee's existing criteria with respect to conflict-related sexual violence and obstruction of humanitarian access. We can support the draft with these adjustments.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia welcomes the strengthened language on sieges, El Fasher and Zamzam camp, and starvation, and remains ready to support the resolution. We still believe the Council must explicitly condemn indiscriminate airstrikes by the Sudanese Armed Forces and demand compliance with international humanitarian law. We also continue to call for explicit cooperation with the International Criminal Court under resolution 1593 (2005), consistent with the Council’s accountability commitments and Slovenia’s consistent position on protection of civilians and ending impunity.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the draft's core focus on ceasefire, humanitarian access and Sudanese sovereignty. We ask the penholder to strengthen the regional coordination language by explicitly including the League of Arab States alongside the AU, IGAD and OIC, and to make clear that any protection-of-civilians recommendations respect Sudan's sovereignty and are implemented with the Government of Sudan's consent. These points reflect Somalia's consistent position on sovereignty and Arab-African solidarity.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: We welcome the inclusion of civilian evacuation from besieged areas, the Adré crossing, and war crimes accountability. We continue to believe the Council should speak more clearly against external support that fuels this conflict and should call on those with influence to bring the parties to the table. We also seek language ensuring the Adré crossing is not only referenced but sustained and predictable in practice. With those amendments, the United Kingdom can support the text.

replies.Algeria: partially accepted: OP8 engagement added and OP3 now applies feasible precautions to all parties while reaffirming Sudan's primary responsibility; no SAF-specific clause.
replies.China: accepted: OP4 recast around facilitation consistent with Sudan's sovereignty and national laws.
replies.Denmark: rejected: ICC/Fact-Finding reference omitted to preserve US position and Council balance.
replies.France: partially accepted: Chapter VII added; ICC reference and OP7 'demands' rejected to avoid Russian veto and maintain balance.
replies.Greece: partially accepted: 'all those responsible' added; ICC reference rejected.
replies.Guyana: partially accepted: OP3 now demands all parties comply with IHL and take precautions; no SAF-specific demand.
replies.Republic of Korea: accepted: no changes requested; Adré and 1591 engagement retained.
replies.Russian Federation: accepted: red-line deletions on OP3/OP7 and consent language in OP4/OP6 incorporated.
replies.Sierra Leone: partially accepted: OP8 criteria added; OP3 applies IHL demands to all parties rather than singling out SAF.
replies.Slovenia: partially accepted: general demands on airstrikes retained; ICC and SAF-specific condemnation rejected.
replies.Somalia: accepted: League of Arab States and consent language added.
replies.United Kingdom: partially accepted: Adré sustained use and influence clause added; 'condemns reports' language omitted due Russian red line.

steps.summary: The revision accommodates Russia's red lines to avoid a veto while retaining strong humanitarian, protection, and sanctions-compliance language. It accepts China's OP4 formulation and adds key sovereignty and accountability safeguards, leaving enough support for adoption with no negative P5 vote.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria had signalled support with changes, and the penholder partially accommodated its key concerns on OP3 and OP8. Voting in favour is consistent with Algeria’s emphasis on humanitarian protection, Sudanese sovereignty, and regional ownership.
reasons.China: China’s key OP4 amendment was accepted, and the text sufficiently safeguards sovereignty, consent, and Sudanese ownership while supporting ceasefire and humanitarian access. This aligns with China’s prior votes and its practice of supporting balanced Council action on Sudan.
reasons.Denmark: Denmark’s overall priorities—ceasefire, humanitarian access, civilian protection, and sanctions—are advanced by the draft, despite the rejected ICC/fact-finding amendment. An abstention would not improve the text and would weaken a unified Council response.
reasons.France: France has consistently supported Security Council action on Sudan, including ceasefire and humanitarian access, and would not block a broadly supported US draft despite the omission of its ICC reference. Voting in favour maintains Council unity while France continues to advocate accountability and stronger language on external interference.
reasons.Greece: Greece had sought an ICC reference but the draft otherwise aligns with its support for humanitarian action, civilian protection, and accountability, and it is likely to vote in favour while registering regret over the rejected ICC language. The urgent crisis and Council unity considerations make abstention or opposition unlikely.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana has consistently supported Council action on Sudan, including ceasefire and humanitarian draft resolutions, and its requested change was partially reflected in OP3. Despite a remaining concern over an explicit SAF-specific demand, the overall draft advances core Guyanese priorities on civilian protection, humanitarian access, sovereignty and accountability, so Guyana votes in favour.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan’s stated position supports ceasefire, humanitarian relief, and Sudanese sovereignty, and it recorded support with no requested changes; voting in favour is consistent with that record.
reasons.Panama: Panama had already signalled support for the draft with no requested changes, and its foreign policy prioritises humanitarian protection, peaceful settlement, sovereignty, and Council unity. Voting in favour is consistent with that stance and with its general support for US-led humanitarian resolutions.
reasons.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea has consistently supported Security Council action on Sudan, including US and UK-led drafts, and the present text reflects its priorities on humanitarian access, civilian protection, sanctions implementation, and respect for Sudanese sovereignty. A vote in favour is consistent with its prior record and its role as Chair of the 1591 Committee.
reasons.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation would likely abstain: its red-line deletions and government-consent language were incorporated, but the text retains Western-favoured accountability and protection-of-civilians language that Moscow views as unbalanced. Abstaining avoids a veto while registering concerns.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supported the draft with changes, and its key OP8 request was accepted; the OP3 language now applies IHL obligations to all parties, which is acceptable though not ideal. Its established policy prioritizes civilian protection, humanitarian access, sovereignty, and African-led processes, making a yes vote likely.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia has consistently supported Security Council action on Sudan and protecting civilians. Despite the absence of its ICC and SAF-specific language, the draft advances ceasefire, humanitarian access, and accountability demands, so Slovenia votes yes while registering reservations.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia had requested important amendments that were accepted, and its vote in favour reflects support for the draft’s humanitarian demands, respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, and strengthened regional coordination.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The UK consistently supports Security Council action on Sudan’s humanitarian crisis and civilian protection, and its key request on sustained Adré access was incorporated. Although the text could be stronger on external arms transfers, London prioritises Council unity and a clear ceasefire and access message.
reasons.United States of America: The United States submitted the draft and its record shows consistent support for Council action on Sudan humanitarian access, civilian protection, ceasefire, and sanctions implementation. It will therefore vote in favour and speak before the vote to urge adoption.

before.Algeria: Algeria votes in favour of this draft resolution. We thank the United States for its efforts and for having taken on board several of our concerns during the negotiations. We support this text because it demands an immediate cessation of hostilities, unimpeded humanitarian access, and the protection of civilians, while reaffirming the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Sudan. We also welcome the recognition of the primary responsibility of the Government of Sudan to protect civilians and the strengthening of engagement with the Government of Sudan and regional partners on the implementation of the measures. At the same time, we reiterate that the response of the Security Council must be guided by full respect for Sudan’s sovereignty and must not place the internationally recognized Government and the Rapid Support Forces on an equal footing. Humanitarian action must be coordinated with and consented to by the Government of Sudan, and international efforts should support a Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led political process in close coordination with the African Union and IGAD.
before.China: Mr. President, China has carefully studied the draft resolution before us. The conflict in Sudan continues to cause grave civilian suffering, and China supports an immediate ceasefire, protection of civilians, and safe, unhindered humanitarian access. At the same time, Council action must respect the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of Sudan and must be based on full consultation with the Government of Sudan. In this regard, we welcome the acceptance of China’s proposal to place humanitarian access in paragraph 4 within the framework of Sudan’s sovereignty and national laws. The draft also reaffirms Sudanese ownership and the consent of the Government of Sudan in relevant processes. On that basis, China will vote in favour of the draft resolution. We call on all parties to cease hostilities and resolve the crisis through dialogue and negotiation, and we urge the international community to support the efforts of the African Union, IGAD and regional countries in a balanced and constructive manner.
before.Denmark: Denmark thanks the penholder for its efforts to negotiate a text that responds to the catastrophic situation in Sudan. We strongly support the demands for an immediate ceasefire, unimpeded humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and full compliance with the sanctions regime. Denmark regrets that the text does not explicitly reference the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan and the International Criminal Court, as accountability for serious international crimes is essential. Nonetheless, given the urgency of the humanitarian crisis and the central importance of the resolution’s demands, Denmark will vote in favour.
before.France: France will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The situation in Sudan is catastrophic, and the Security Council must demand an immediate ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian access and the protection of civilians. France welcomes the inclusion of Chapter VII and the reaffirmation of the sanctions measures. We regret that the text does not explicitly recall the role of the International Criminal Court with respect to Darfur, because accountability is essential to break the cycle of impunity. France nevertheless supports the adoption of this resolution and urges all parties to implement it without delay.
before.Greece: Greece votes in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian catastrophe in Sudan and the continuing grave violations demand urgent Council action, including demands for a ceasefire, the protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, and accountability. Greece regrets that the text does not explicitly reference the International Criminal Court, given our strong commitment to ending impunity for serious international crimes. We welcome the addition of “all those responsible” and will continue to advocate that accountability efforts, including through the ICC where appropriate, are upheld.
before.Guyana: Guyana thanks the penholder for its efforts. My delegation will vote in favour of this draft. The situation in Sudan demands urgent Council action: cessation of hostilities, unimpeded humanitarian access, protection of civilians and civilian objects, accountability for serious violations, and respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. Guyana supported this text because it sends a clear message that all parties must comply with international humanitarian law and human rights law. We would have preferred an explicit and direct demand on all parties, including the Sudanese Armed Forces, to take all feasible precautions to avoid civilian harm, but we recognize that the draft now demands compliance by all parties. We urge full implementation, including safe humanitarian access through all available routes and the protection of humanitarian personnel. Guyana remains committed to a Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led political process and to the full, equal and meaningful participation of women, youth and civil society.
before.Pakistan: Pakistan will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We support its call for an immediate ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and a Sudanese-owned political process that respects the sovereignty, unity, independence, and territorial integrity of Sudan. Pakistan urges all parties to de-escalate, facilitate relief to those in need, and return to dialogue through regional and international mediation, while ensuring that international efforts are undertaken in full respect for Sudan’s sovereignty and with close coordination with the Government of Sudan and regional organizations.
before.Panama: Panama votes in favour of this draft resolution. The humanitarian catastrophe in Sudan, including famine, mass displacement and attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, requires the Council to speak clearly and act with urgency. We support the demands for a nationwide ceasefire, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, respect for Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a credible Sudanese-led political process. Panama remains committed to accountability and to the full implementation of this Council’s decisions.
before.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea votes in favour of this draft resolution. We support the Council’s clear demands for an immediate ceasefire, the protection of civilians, and safe, timely, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access, including through the Adré crossing. We stress the importance of full compliance with the arms embargo and the measures reaffirmed in resolution 2750 (2024), and we welcome the continued engagement of the 1591 Committee. We also emphasize that all efforts must respect Sudan’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity and be pursued in close coordination with the Government of Sudan and regional partners, while ensuring accountability for serious violations. We urge all parties to return to negotiations without preconditions and to translate their commitments into meaningful progress on the ground.
before.Russian Federation: Mr. President, the Russian Federation will abstain on this draft resolution. We note that the penholder has taken into account a number of our principled proposals, including the need to respect the consent of the Government of Sudan and to avoid imposing external prescriptions on Sudan. At the same time, the text still contains unbalanced assessments and provisions that go beyond the Council’s mandate, including language that could be used to justify external interference in Sudan’s internal affairs. We believe the Council’s efforts should concentrate on supporting a genuinely Sudanese-led political process, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and an end to external support that fuels the conflict.
before.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The situation in Sudan demands urgent Council action: civilians are being killed and displaced, famine conditions are spreading, and humanitarian access remains constrained. We welcome the text’s clear demands for a nationwide ceasefire, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, and full compliance with international humanitarian law by all parties. We also welcome the inclusion of listing criteria related to conflict-related sexual violence and obstruction of humanitarian access, reflecting an important priority for Sierra Leone. While we would have preferred an equally explicit and strong formulation regarding the obligations of the Sudanese Armed Forces, we take note that the revised text applies international humanitarian law demands to all parties. Sierra Leone remains firmly committed to Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, independence and territorial integrity, and to a Sudanese-owned political process with the full and meaningful participation of women, youth and civil society. We urge all parties to comply with this resolution and call upon the Council to remain seized of the matter.
before.Slovenia:
Slovenia will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The Security Council must not remain silent while civilians in Sudan continue to suffer grave violence, displacement, hunger and attacks on essential infrastructure. We support the resolution’s demands for a ceasefire, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and full compliance with international humanitarian law and the sanctions regime.

At the same time, we regret that our proposals were not retained. We stress that all parties, including the Sudanese Armed Forces, must comply with international humanitarian law and refrain from indiscriminate airstrikes. Those responsible for war crimes and other serious violations must be held accountable, and cooperation with the International Criminal Court consistent with resolution 1593 (2005) remains essential. We call for the full implementation of this resolution.
before.Somalia: Mr. President, Somalia will vote in favour of this resolution. We welcome the incorporation of our proposals to include the League of Arab States and to affirm that any recommendations respect Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and are implemented with the consent of the Government of Sudan. We urge all parties to cease hostilities, protect civilians, and ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access, and we support a Sudanese-owned political process with close regional coordination.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports this resolution and will vote in favour. The Sudanese people have endured nearly two years of conflict and a humanitarian catastrophe, and this Council must speak clearly. We welcome the demands for an immediate ceasefire, for safe and unhindered humanitarian access, including through the Adré crossing, and for the protection of civilians, including in El Fasher and Zamzam. We also call on all Member States to refrain from actions that fuel the conflict and to comply with the arms embargo. The United Kingdom urges all members of this Council to support the text and to send a united message that the suffering of the Sudanese people must end.
before.United States of America: The United States strongly supports this draft resolution and urges all Council members to vote in favour. The situation in Sudan demands that this Council speak with one voice: we call for an immediate nationwide ceasefire, the protection of civilians, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, accountability for serious violations, and strict compliance with the arms embargo. This text also respects Sudan’s sovereignty and the role of the Government of Sudan, while making clear that all parties — especially the Rapid Support Forces and allied militias — must halt attacks on civilians, lift sieges, and allow life-saving aid to reach those in need. The United States thanks all partners who engaged constructively and calls for the resolution’s adoption.

after.China:
Mr. President,

China welcomes the adoption of the resolution. The conflict in Sudan has caused severe civilian suffering, and the Security Council must send a clear and urgent message on ceasefire, protection of civilians and humanitarian access. China voted in favour because the text, as revised, reaffirms the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Sudan and recognizes the role and consent of the Government of Sudan in humanitarian and political processes. These elements are important to China.

We call on all parties to the conflict to genuinely implement the resolution, cease hostilities, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and ensure safe, timely and unhindered humanitarian access. At the same time, the Council’s actions must remain objective and impartial, avoid external imposition, and respect Sudan’s ownership. China supports a Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned political process, with the constructive role of the African Union, IGAD, the League of Arab States and other regional partners, as well as the good offices of the Secretary-General and his Personal Envoy. The international community should continue to provide humanitarian assistance and support a political settlement, rather than complicating the situation through interference. China will continue to play a constructive role in this regard.
after.United States of America:
Thank you, Mr. President.

The United States welcomes the adoption of this resolution and thanks the members of the Council who voted in favour. Today the Security Council has sent a clear and united message: the fighting in Sudan must stop, civilians must be protected, and life-saving humanitarian aid must reach those in need without obstruction.

This resolution demands a durable, nationwide ceasefire; it demands that all parties—including the Rapid Support Forces and allied militias—halt attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, lift sieges, and respect international humanitarian law. It reaffirms the sanctions measures and arms embargo, and it makes clear that accountability for serious violations matters. It also fully respects Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, independence, and territorial integrity.

We note that Russia abstained. An abstention is not a neutral act when civilians are suffering and the Council is being asked to act. We call on all Member States to support implementation of this resolution and to avoid any action that fuels the conflict.

The United States remains committed to the Sudanese people and will continue to work with the Government of Sudan, regional partners, and this Council to advance peace, protection, and accountability. Adoption is an important step—now implementation is what must follow.
